White House recasts Trump arch as military tribute

Reuters

07 November, 2026 01:00 am IST

By Bo Erickson WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) – Hours after a US judge paused construction on President Donald Trump’s proposed 250-foot (76.2-meter) arch in Washington, the White House on Friday shared new depictions portraying the project as a tribute to the nation’s military heritage, the latest attempt to rebrand it amid mounting opposition.

The site unveiled on Friday calls the project, which would stand near the entrance of Arlington National Cemetery, the Military Triumphal Arch.

Animated images show a trio of gilded, winged statues above the words “GOLDEN AGE OF AMERICA,” written in gold letters set against stone. A flame emanates from a torch in the hands of one of the winged female figures.

Show Full Article

The White House shared the new renderings from a group called the United States Triumphal Arch Foundation. Its listed chairman, former Trump-appointed ambassador Randy Evans, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump has increasingly turned his attention to a series of major projects in Washington, both before and after his Republican Party suffered massive losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections that cost the party control of Congress.

The arch and Trump’s other signature projects have drawn significant political and legal opposition.

The attorneys general from Virginia and the District of Columbia have sued to prevent construction of the arch, which they say will irreparably damage the skyline of the nation’s capital and surrounding area, including Arlington National Cemetery, the nation’s most revered resting ground for service men and women, and the nearby Lincoln Memorial.

Some aviation experts also raised safety concerns given its proximity to Reagan Washington National Airport. However, the Federal Aviation Administration greenlit the project in September.

The president previously justified the arch as a “military complex” to be used for drones and snipers. The new renderings indicate the arch is also now dedicated to the nation’s military history.

The National Capital Planning Commission, a regional authority, voted on Thursday to approve the arch project after hearing from about 100 opponents, including Democratic lawmakers. Hours later, US District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day restraining order on construction, saying it would last about three years and “disrupt traffic, create noise, result in large-scale excavation, and more.”

The Trump administration contends Congress approved the arch more than 100 years ago when it also authorized construction of a bridge across the Potomac River.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle on Friday said the federal ruling came from “an activist district court” and added, “We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch — a tribute to 250 years of American greatness.”

Construction is expected to take two to three years, according to Interior Department documents submitted to the planning commission on Thursday.

(Reporting by Bo EricksonEditing by Bill Berkrot)

By Vincent Mumo Nzilani and Jefferson Kahinju MOMBASA, Kenya, Nov 6 (Reuters) – A Kenyan court sentenced cult leader Paul Mackenzie on Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children starved to death on his orders and buried in a forest, among 500 suspected victims of one of the deadliest cult-related mass killings of modern times.

The sentence comprised 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years for direct homicide, Justice Diana Kavedza said, reading out the judgement.

Prosecutors said Mackenzie, who led an apocalyptic Christian church in a forest near eastern Kenya’s Indian Ocean coast, had told his followers to starve themselves to death, along with their children, to reach heaven before the end of the world.

Show Full Article

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie, wearing a grey polo shirt and black trousers, did not react as the judge read out his sentence in a tent set up outside the court where the hearing was held.

He had denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve. The court rejected his defence.

Twenty-eight accomplices received sentences ranging from 10 to 160 years. All were found guilty at a trial last month.

Defence lawyer Lawrence Obonyo, who represents Mackenzie and almost all of the others convicted, said he would appeal the ruling.

Mackenzie, who broadcast sermons on a YouTube channel that had thousands of subscribers, won the trust of his victims through his charismatic media presence and then targeted defenceless, vulnerable followers, particularly children, Kavedza said.

“Children observed as their siblings dropped dead after enduring hunger for days,” she said. “Those who stole food or water were beaten, their hands tied and locked up in houses, turned into fasting bays to die.”

FATHERS LOST SIX CHILDREN

The case shocked Kenya in April 2023, when police began uncovering bodies in Shakahola Forest near the coastal town of Malindi.

Although only the cases of 190 children and one adult victim were covered by the trial, the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights says 448 bodies were ultimately found in the forest.

Mackenzie is also accused of ordering the deaths of 52 people found at a separate location in a village 30 km (18 miles) away, bringing the suspected total toll to 500. He has pleaded not guilty in that case.

The scale of the killing is comparable to that of a doomsday cult that killed more than 700 people in Uganda in 2000, and the 1978 Jonestown massacre in Guyana, when an American cult leader killed more than 900 people by ordering them to drink poison.

Stephen Mwiti, 48, father of six of Mackenzie’s child victims and husband of one of his convicted accomplices, said his wife had taken the children to Shakahola, where they were starved to death.

Even if the adults had agreed to fast, “what about the children?” Mwiti told Reuters ahead of the sentencing.

Suleiman Zero, whose wife and six children are still missing, wept outside court after the sentencing. “I am happy but where is my family?” he said. “The one thing that I request from the government is that they help find my family. If they are dead, then let me have the bodies to bury.”

Dan Mackenzie, one of Paul Mackenzie’s sons, said he fled the group in his early teens after he stopped believing its promises of heaven, and lost friends and his younger brother there.

“It’s justice to the people who we lost over there in Shakahola,” he said.

AN IMPORTANT STEP, BUT MORE ACCOUNTABILITY NEEDED

Mackenzie had been on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church in Malindi and he relocated to the nearby Shakahola Forest.

The discoveries prompted calls for tighter oversight of religious groups, but government-backed and Senate proposals have yet to become law.

Ojiro Odhiambo, head of rapid response at the Kenya Human Rights Commission, said the conviction was an important step but accountability should go further as local administrators, police, intelligence officers and religious leaders bore responsibility for failing to act on repeated warning signs.

“All these people have failed the people,” he said.

Kavedza agreed that Kenyan institutions had failed and she called for parliament to take steps to prevent it from happening again.

In 2023, Ruto said he took responsibility as president for the government having failed to prevent the deaths.

(Reporting by Vincent Mumo Nzilani in Mombasa, Jeff Kahinju and Nelson Aruya in Malindi and Edwin Okoth and George Obulutsa in Nairobi;Writing by David Lewis; Editing by Peter Graff and Xevi Fontdegloria)

BARCELONA, Nov 6 (Reuters) – China is in contact with Real Madrid and LaLiga over the fallout from Kylian Mbappe’s remarks about Mao Zedong, China’s ambassador to Spain Yao Jing said on Friday.

“There are no negotiations, but there is communication, based on mutual understanding,” Yao told Spanish news agency EFE before attending a forum at the University of Salamanca.

“This unfortunate incident hurt the feelings of many people in China, who now have to come to terms with the current situation,” he added.

Show Full Article

The dispute began after a video circulated online in which the Real Madrid and France forward discussed a meme showing his face superimposed on an image of Mao.

Mbappe described the figure as “some guy, I think he’s a Chinese dictator” but did not name Mao, modern China’s founding leader who governed the country from 1949 until his death in 1976.

LaLiga, Real Madrid and the French footballer all subsequently apologised.

China’s state broadcaster CCTV suspended its coverage of LaLiga and several Chinese brands dropped Mbappe from their marketing campaigns.

Streaming platform Migu omitted Real Madrid’s match against Racing Santander last weekend while showing other Spanish league games.

China Media Group said last week that it would listen to what Mbappe had to say after his apology, and “more importantly” watch what he does.

LaLiga president Javier Tebas met Yao last week as Spanish football sought to limit the commercial fallout and said on Monday that the league was continuing its dialogue with Chinese authorities.

LaLiga was “working to resolve it”, Tebas said at the World In Progress forum, adding that it continued to have an “extraordinary relationship” with CCTV and Migu.

LaLiga and Migu have an agreement allowing the broadcast of Spain’s top division matches until the end of the 2029-30 season.

The LaLiga president said the league’s broadcasting contracts with CCTV and Migu totalled around €10 million ($11.20 million) per year, having fallen from €100 million annually at their peak.

Real Madrid did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

($1 = 0.8930 euros)

(Reporting by Ruairidh BarlowEditing by Toby Davis)

By Sfundo Parakozov and Anathi Madubela JOHANNESBURG, Nov 6 (Reuters) – South Africa’s African National Congress was heading for major losses in municipal elections, results showed on Friday, setting the stage for multi-party coalition battles to control Johannesburg and other major conurbations.

With 81% of votes counted by 1130 GMT, the ANC had 32% against 25% for its main rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA).

If that holds, the party that has dominated South African politics since the end of apartheid would shed about 14 percentage points from the 2021 municipal election, which was, at the time, its worst local result on record.

Show Full Article

It would mark a further erosion in the ANC’s grip on power after it lost its national parliamentary majority in 2024.

The party of the late anti-apartheid icon Nelson Mandela has seen its support dwindle amid high unemployment and crime, corruption scandals and anger over failing water, electricity and other services.

The DA was on course for an outright majority in Cape Town, and has emerged in stronger positions elsewhere, setting up complex negotiations in which smaller parties including ActionSA could hold considerable sway.

DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis said his party had already begun contacting potential coalition partners.

“We will approach the next few weeks with respect for the mandates those parties have received from their voters, and humility, and a commitment to trying to put together governments that get those towns and cities working,” he said.

Political analyst Ralph Mathekga said the DA’s most straightforward path to stable governments could be deals with the ANC, its partner in the national government, but that risked alienating voters who had just punished the ANC.

“I think if voters wanted the ANC to be back in municipalities, they would have voted for the ANC,” Mathekga said.

ActionSA, a party founded in 2020 by former Johannesburg mayor Herman Mashaba, is also positioning itself as a potential kingmaker, particularly in Gauteng Province.

It says it is prepared to negotiate across the political spectrum if parties agree on improving basic services, stabilising councils and fighting corruption.

“Ultimately, I’m quite convinced no government is going to be formed without us,” its national chairperson, Michael Beaumont, said.

As vote tallying enters the final stages, the outcome remains unclear in eThekwini, the municipality centred on the port-city of Durban, where former President Jacob Zuma is hoping his party — a splinter from the ANC — can seize a majority.

(Reporting by Sfundo Parakozov, Anthi Madubela and Nilutpal Timsina; Writing by Alexander Winning; Editing by Bate Felix, William Mallard and Andrew Heavens)
